# Independent audit: exact depth of a simplex with small corner truncations


candidate 3795aff5f3322d52,
including Sections 1 and 5-7 in addition to the previously separately
audited central argument. Its verifier reran successfully: 1181
exact defining-equation, weight, derivative, and closed-form checks.
No correction is required.

## All-direction reduction and uniform smallness

For a fixed standard simplex the unperturbed cap-volume function
is jointly continuous in the candidate and unit normal. The only
centroid equality normals are the canonical apex-side directions.
Small disjoint normal neighborhoods therefore leave a positive
compact gap outside them. Shrinking the candidate neighborhood
keeps this gap and the strict one-positive-vertex sign patterns.

In the vertex-i chamber, the hyperplane coefficients satisfy
a_j>1 and sum a_j lambda_j(y)=1. AM-GM yields the exact least
volume d^d product_(j!=i)lambda_j(y), attained by
a_j=1/(d lambda_j(y)). These coefficients remain in the chamber
for candidates sufficiently near the centroid.

Disjointness and volumes of the deleted corners are exact.
The original centroid's depth is at least (G-t)V after deletion.
At every truncated-body maximizer the canonical upper bounds
therefore force all barycentrics uniformly to 1/(d+1) as t->0.
Thus every maximizer enters the chosen candidate neighborhood.

The same uniform cap gap survives deletion of total mass tV.
Within each canonical normal neighborhood, strict vertex signs
and sufficiently small corner diameters put the whole i-th
deleted corner inside the cap and every other deleted corner
outside it. Consequently the deleted mass there is exactly t_i V,
independent of the normal. This proves the local all-normal
formula rather than assuming that the old facet-parallel caps
alone minimize depth.

All choices can be made in a fixed order in the standard simplex:
normal neighborhoods, a smaller candidate neighborhood, and then
a common bound on every epsilon_i. This supplies a dimension-only
epsilon_* uniformly over relative truncation sizes. Affine
invariance transports it to arbitrary simplices.

## Scalar root and unique global maximizing point

At the origin of parameter space the scalar equation has
F(D,0)=m^d D-d^d and positive D-derivative m^d. Uniform endpoint
signs and strict monotonicity near G give exactly one nearby
positive root, with smooth parameter dependence.

The defining equation gives d^d product lambda_i^*=c and hence
d^d product_(j!=i)lambda_j^*-t_i=D for every i. For small
parameters the candidate is inside K and the weights
w_i=1-d lambda_i^* are positive and sum to one.

If another positive barycentric vector had all its local cap
values at least D, every product of the corresponding ratios
excluding one index would be at least one. Weighting their
logarithms by w_i gives a nonnegative quantity equal to
d sum lambda_j^* log r_j. Strict Jensen bounds it above by zero,
with equality only when every r_j=1. This proves uniqueness of
the local optimum, not merely first-order stationarity.
Localization of every global maximizer then proves the global
claim and the all-containing-halfspace lower bound.

## Closed forms, derivatives, and boundary cases

The one-corner equations follow by equating the truncated apex
value with the untruncated other-vertex values. In dimension two
they give b=(1+sqrt(1+3t))/6 and
D=2(1+sqrt(1+3t))/9-2t/3. In particular the other optimal normals
are generally tilted; using their old canonical cap formulas
would not give the stated exact answer.

The logarithmic expansion yields
D'=-sum tau_i/m and quadratic coefficient
-(d-1)sum(tau_i-mean tau)^2/(2mG).
The printed barycentric displacement and normalization by
1-s sum tau_i have the correct constants and signs. Equal
corner volumes give exactly uniform barycentrics and D=G-t/m.

For d=1 the scalar equation reduces to 2D+t_0+t_1=1 and the
candidate is the actual interval midpoint, valid throughout
epsilon_0+epsilon_1<1. Individual zero truncations are harmless;
the all-zero vector returns the original simplex. Every relevant
continuous hyperplane is Lebesgue-null, and the source keeps the
closed inequalities. No additional boundary mass or exchange
of an optimizer with a limit is needed.

This is an ordinary convex-body theorem. The proof and this audit
make no mixed-source allocation or general OC inference.
